name: Unfiltered Stories
_comment_group: One of the shows under the Snapchat heading, built to Hall of Femme's
brief: a frame fetcher rather than a thumbnail maker, captioned with
what was being said, the caption set on a card in colours the user
Everything that makes it a Snapchat pack is stated in the same three
references its sibling uses - the frame fetch, the framing profile and
the caption design - so what is left in this file is the four things
that make it this show: the face, the second face a picked word is set
in, the colour of the card, and the palette behind both.
The two faces are where it parts company with Hall of Femme, and not
only by being different files. That show sets its highlight in the
other END of one family, 200 against 800, so a picked word is the same
letterforms under more ink. This one crosses families: a wide geometric
medium, picked out in an ultra condensed bold. See the highlight note
below, which is where that costs something and says what.

_comment_face: New Order Medium. A wide geometric with a circular O and a W a
full em across, which is the opposite build from the condensed
display faces most of this heading is set in - the letters are
generous rather than packed, and a caption in them reads as
something typeset rather than as something shouted.
It costs the line what it gains in the letterform, and the number
is worth knowing before the preset's maxChars is ever touched: its
capitals average 0.620em, so twenty of them at the preset's 40px
are 496px against the 486px the block is given. A twenty-character
line of solid capitals would therefore be the one width this face
cannot hold - it does not happen because real lines carry spaces,
which are narrower than the average capital and pull a full line
back to around 450px, but the margin is thin enough that raising
maxChars here would break lines the width has to break again.
A Medium rather than something heavier, and the card is what makes
that possible - the same argument Hall of Femme makes for being
able to set a hairline. A 500-weight face over an unknown
photograph is a caption that disappears on a blown-out sky; on a
card of its own it has a background somebody chose, and the weight
becomes a choice instead of a risk.
_comment_color: The channel's own answer, and therefore what every frame is set in
until somebody presses a swatch: a frame stores no colour of its
own until it is given one, and this is what it falls back to (see
state.textColorFor). It is one of the five in `colors` below - the
second of them, so the swatch that shows as chosen on an untouched
frame is not the one at the start of the row, which nothing
requires: the swatch is found by matching this value rather than
by being listed first.
Absolute black, and it is the second answer this key has had. The
show opened on absolute white, as the brand stated it, and the
numbers against the card it opens on are unusual enough to be
worth keeping written down: #FFFFFF on #F9F268 is a contrast ratio
of 1.17:1, and at that ratio the letters are not faint, they are
gone. Four of the five colours in this palette are light (see the
note below), so that opening pairing was two of them, and the
frame came up as a yellow card with the caption legible only where
it overlapped nothing.
Black on the same card is 17.93:1 and is now what the show opens
on. It was always one key - nothing else in the pack depends on
which of the five this is - and the white is still one press away
for anyone who wants the brand's own answer on a frame that can
carry it.
_comment_colors: The five colours this show is set in, offered for the letters and
for the card behind them - five buttons each in the title panel
(see editor.renderColorButtons). The same five in both lists,
deliberately, and for Hall of Femme's reason: what the show is set
in is the PAIRING, so what is offered is twenty-five combinations
rather than five cards.
The five are not five equals, though, and this is the one thing to
know before reading the row as a palette. One of them is absolute
black and the other four are light - a white, a butter yellow at
0.85 luminance, a lilac at 0.55 and a mint at 0.74. Contrast runs
across that line and nowhere else. Black against the four lights is
21.00, 17.93, 12.04 and 15.89 to one; every pairing of two lights is
between 1.13 and 1.74, which is a caption nobody can read at arm's
length or at any other length.
So eight of the twenty-five combinations are captions and the rest
are a card with something on it. That is stated rather than designed
around: the two lists stay independent, as they are on every pack
under this heading, because the pairing is the feature and a rule
barring the seventeen would cost the panel more explaining than an
unreadable caption costs the user, who can see it is unreadable and
presses another swatch. Hall of Femme makes the same argument about
the four ways of setting a colour on itself; here it simply covers
more of the grid.
The order is the brand's own and is not sorted by anything. It
happens to open each row on that row's default - white first for the
letters - except the card's, whose #F9F268 is third; the two rows
are written identically and the chosen swatch is found by matching,
so neither position means anything (see `panel` below).
`text` reaches the highlight as well as the block - see the note on
`colors` in js/channels.js. This channel's highlight is a different
FACE and not a different colour, so what colour the type is has one
answer and not two.
_comment_highlight: A picked word is set in Mongoose Bold, in the same colour as the
rest of the block. The highlight here is WIDTH: an ultra condensed
bold inside a wide geometric medium, which on one line is as loud as
a box would be and leaves the card one clean shape instead of a
shape with a second shape inside it.
The colour it names is the block's, so the recolour draws exactly
what its neighbours are drawn in and the face is the whole of the
difference. Stated all the same, for the fallback reason `color`
above is stated - and moved to black with it, since a highlight
that changed colour as well as face would be two highlights.
The mode and the scope come from the preset, which is where the
argument for picking out words rather than lines lives. What is this
channel's own is how FAR apart the two faces are, and it has three
consequences the pack should own rather than discover:
A picked word is about 48% of the width the same word would be in
the block's face - 0.300em of capital against 0.620em. That is the
effect, and it is also why the card moves: the panel is drawn one
box per line, cut to each line's own measured width (see
`panel.scope` in the preset), so picking two words out of a line
visibly pulls that line's box in. On a joined panel the shape steps
further in and out with the sentence than it does on any sibling.
A picked word is also slightly SHORTER. Mongoose's capitals stand at
0.680em against New Order's 0.733, so at the one stated size of 40px
the picked run is around 7% lower than the capitals either side of
it, sitting on the same baseline. Between two faces this unlike,
that reads as the second voice it is meant to be rather than as a
size that slipped - and it is not adjustable in any case: a block
takes one size, and the renderer has no per-highlight size to give
(see `highlight.face` in content/README.md).
And two picked words in a row are set tight. Neighbouring picked
words are ONE run with the space between them inside it (see
treatmentRuns in js/text.js), so that space is Mongoose's own
0.080em - 3.2px at 40px, against the 10px the block's face sets. It
is the condensed face's own spacing and it is right for the
condensed face; it simply means a picked phrase reads as one word
more than a picked word does. The space on either side of a run
belongs to the unpicked side and is the block's, so a single picked
word keeps its ordinary word spaces.
_comment_panel: Butter yellow, and the fill is the one thing about the card this
pack decides: its shape, its padding, its corners and its shadow are
the Snapchat caption design and come from the preset.
It is the third entry in `colors.panel` above rather than the first,
and that is not an oversight. The two rows are written in the
brand's own order, identically, and the swatch that shows as chosen
is whichever one matches this value - so the card can open on the
third button while the type opens on the first without either row
The card is also the reason the preset can drop every drop shadow
behind the letters: there is no photograph under them to hold them
off. What lifts the caption off the still is the shadow the card
itself casts, which is the preset's and is the same on every channel

_comment_branding: No dark gradient. It exists to hold a title legible against the
photograph, and this title is not against the photograph at all - it is
on a card of its own. A scrim over every still would darken forty
pictures to solve a problem the card has already solved.
